newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia approves law clamping down on contraband.
newsitem.headline: Colombia approves law clamping down on contraband.

text.p: Colombia's Congress has passed a law aimed at cutting the booming trade in contraband goods, much of which is known to be controlled by drug kingpins.

The law, mandating prison sentences of three to six years for virtually anyone caught trafficking in large quantities of contraband, was approved in an extraordinary session of Congress late on Tuesday. It had failed to win approval in the regular session of Congress, which ended on Friday amid acrimonious debate over the issue of prison sentences.

As drafted by the lower house, the law would have ruled out prison terms in cases involving contraband items valued at less than $170,000. But the Senate beefed it up to ensure that anyone caught smuggling large amounts of contraband into Colombia would face a minimum of three years imprisonment.

According to independent estimates, Colombia's trade in contraband is worth billions of dollars a year, and drug experts say it has long been known as the system of choice for converting drug dollars into local currency.

Traffickers take advantage of the same routes they use to export cocaine and heroin to smuggle in contraband cigarettes, Scotch whisky or electrical appliances bought with their drug dollars in the Caribbean or the United States. Most of the goods are then sold in illicit markets known as Sanandresitos that have cropped up across the country since the 1970s.

Although drug-related contraband has hurt legitimate business and was cited by business leaders as a driving force behind the recession in the first quarter of the year, authorities have long turned a blind eye to the practice.

President Ernesto Samper, whose alleged ties to the Cali drug cartel triggered Colombia's worst political crisis in decades, was named "honorary president" of the federation that represents owners of the country's Sanandresitos before he was elected president in 1994.
